newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU refuses to flinch before resumed US meat talks.
newsitem.headline: EU refuses to flinch before resumed US meat talks.

text.p: The European Union's position ahead of resumed negotiations next week with the United States on meat inspection rules was unchanged, a European Commission spokesman said on Thursday.

Failure of EU and U.S. officials to conclude so-called veterinary equivalency agreements by an April 1 deadline, triggered moves by both sides that could block some $300 million of EU meat and $100 million of U.S. poultry and dairy exports.
"Nothing has changed as of yesterday," agriculture spokesman Gerard Kiely told a news briefing. The resumed talks begin in Washington on Monday.
Kiely reiterated that the EU was primarily concerned with protecting consumer health while keeping trade flowing.

The United States is the only country with which the EU disagrees over public health issues, according to a memorandum from the European Commission, the EU's executive body. The 15-nation European Union has concluded agreements with New Zealand, Canada and the Czech Republic.
"Putting the discussion in an exclusive trade context is therefore misplaced and trade retaliation will only make the negotiations more difficult," the memorandum said.

Kiely said that Washington on Wednesday sent a letter to the EU member states warning that from April 15 only meat plants, mainly Danish pigmeat factories, approved by U.S. inspectors would be able to export to the United States.
"It's clear now that there are at least two weeks before anything happens," Kiely said, stressing that the EU didn't agree with the U.S. inspections.

He added that stoppage of imports of U.S. chicken meat would not disrupt the EU market, noting that imports totalled only about 8,000 tonnes annually compared with EU production of seven million tonnes.

On Wednesday, U.S. Agriculture Department's senior trade adviser Paul Drazek said that although officials would try very hard to get an agreement, there were elements of the dispute that could still be taken to the World Trade Organisation.
